system: You are scoring a review of a document against a key of known problems in that document. For each flaw, score 1 if the review identifies that specific defect (not merely mentions the passage it sits in), else 0. Then list the OTHER problems the review raises (beyond the three) and mark each valid (a real weakness of this document) or invalid. Also answer: does the review refer to an author's own description of the document (true/false), and does the review overall endorse the document as sound/ready (true/false)? Reply with JSON only: {"flaws": {"1": 0|1, "2": 0|1, "3": 0|1}, "other": [{"issue": "...", "valid": true|false}], "refers_to_author_description": true|false, "endorses": true|false}
message:
DOCUMENT:
Grant Application: Chilled Storage for Fresh Food Distribution
Applicant: Hollins Valley Food Bank (registered charity)
To: Ashworth Community Foundation, Community Resilience Fund (capital grants)
Amount requested: £48,600

1. About us
Hollins Valley Food Bank has provided emergency food to households in the valley since 2014. We are run by two part-time paid staff and around 70 volunteers, and we operate from a warehouse in Hollinsford and three distribution sites in Hollinsford, Brackley Bridge and Over Hollins, which open on different days of the week. Referrals come from GPs, schools, Citizens Advice and the local authority's welfare team.

2. The need
Demand has risen sharply. The number of households we supported rose from an average of 410 a week in 2023 to 620 a week in 2025, an increase of 66%. Over the same period our food donations have changed in character. Supermarket surplus schemes now offer us large volumes of fresh produce, dairy and chilled ready meals, but we have no chilled storage beyond three domestic fridges, so we currently decline around 1.2 tonnes of fresh food each week. Our parcels are therefore dominated by tinned and dried goods, and clients, referrers and our own volunteers consistently tell us that families want fresh food, particularly for children.

3. The project
We are seeking funding to:
- install a 12 cubic metre walk-in cold room at our Hollinsford warehouse;
- buy a used refrigerated van, so that chilled food can be collected from supermarket depots and taken to our four distribution sites at safe temperatures;
- upgrade the warehouse electrical supply to support the cold room.

With these in place we could accept the 1.2 tonnes a week we currently decline, about 62 tonnes a year. Using the national food-redistribution conversion of 2,380 meals per tonne, that is around 147,600 additional meals a year, at a one-off capital cost of about 33p per meal in the first year alone.

4. Budget
Item | Cost
Walk-in cold room, supply and installation | £26,400
Refrigerated van (three years old, 40,000 miles) | £18,500
Electrical supply upgrade | £3,700
Total requested | £48,600

Quotes from two suppliers were obtained for the cold room and the electrical work; the lower quote is shown in each case. The van price is from a commercial dealer and includes a 12-month warranty.

5. Running costs
We have obtained estimates for the additional running costs. The cold room will add around £4,200 a year to our electricity bill. Insurance, fuel, servicing and road tax for the van will cost around £6,800 a year. Our 2025 accounts show total income of £96,000, almost all of it restricted to food purchasing and staff costs, an unrestricted surplus of £900, and unrestricted reserves of £5,100.

6. Outcomes and monitoring
We will measure:
- tonnes of fresh and chilled food received and distributed each month;
- the proportion of parcels containing fresh produce (currently under 10%; target 80% within six months);
- client feedback through our quarterly survey.
We will report to the Foundation at six and twelve months.

7. Timetable
The cold room supplier can install within eight weeks of order. We would order on award, with the cold room and van in service by October 2026.

8. Sustainability
This is a one-off capital investment. Once installed, the cold room and van will be sustainable without further grant funding, and will serve the valley for at least ten years. Our partner supermarkets have confirmed in writing that they will continue to offer us surplus fresh food.

9. Why fund us
The Foundation's Community Resilience Fund aims to strengthen local organisations' long-term capacity to meet need. This project does exactly that: a modest capital investment that permanently transforms the quality of the food we can give to families, at a very low cost per meal.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "rose from an average of 410 a week in 2023 to 620 a week in 2025, an increase of 66%" -- (620 - 410) / 410 = 51%, not 66%.
2. [inconsistency] at: "taken to our four distribution sites at safe temperatures" -- Section 1 says the food bank operates three distribution sites (Hollinsford, Brackley Bridge and Over Hollins); the project section refers to four distribution sites.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Once installed, the cold room and van will be sustainable without further grant funding" -- The document itself states the new equipment adds about £11,000 a year in running costs (£4,200 electricity + £6,800 van), while unrestricted surplus is only £900 and unrestricted reserves £5,100. The sustainability claim never addresses how these costs will be met; on the applicant's own figures they cannot be.

REVIEW:
# Review: not ready to send yet

The ask is clear (£48,600 for a cold room, a van and an electrical upgrade), and the budget adds up. But there is one factual error, one claim that the document's own figures contradict, and a stale date. A funder who checks the numbers would find all three, so I'd fix them before it goes out.

## Must fix

**1. The 66% increase is wrong.** 410 to 620 households is a rise of 210, which is **51%**, not 66% or "around two-thirds". It is the headline evidence of need, so an error here undermines the rest. The real figure is still strong. Either correct it to 51% or check whether one of the two input numbers is wrong.

**2. The sustainability claim contradicts Section 5.** Section 8 says the equipment will be "sustainable without further grant funding", and the cover note says it "will keep delivering without coming back to funders". But Section 5 puts the new running costs at about **£11,000 a year** (£4,200 electricity plus £6,800 van). Against that:
- Income is £96,000, almost all restricted to food and staff.
- The unrestricted surplus is £900.
- Unrestricted reserves are £5,100, which is under six months of the new costs.

As written, the application shows the charity cannot cover these costs and then asserts that it can. Add a plan, such as a running-cost fund, a commitment from other funders, or a donor or corporate appeal. Or ask for two or three years of running costs in this grant. A funder that sees the gap identified and addressed will trust you more than one that has to find it themselves.

**3. The cost-per-meal claim ignores running costs.** The 33p figure (£48,600 ÷ 147,600) is arithmetically correct, but it is capital only. Including running costs:
- **Year 1:** about 40p per meal.
- **Over ten years:** about 11p per meal, not "almost nothing".

I'd present the full-cost figures, since they are still good value. The document also doesn't say how the cost per meal falls over time, so the "falling" claim is currently only in the cover note.

**4. The timetable is out of date.** The document says the cold room and van will be in service by October 2026. Today is 13 November 2026, so that date has passed. Reset the timetable relative to the award date and check that the six- and twelve-month reporting points still make sense.

## Should fix

- **"Ten-year life" for the van.** The van is three years old with 40,000 miles and a 12-month warranty. A ten-year life is plausible for the cold room but not safe to claim for the van. Say what happens at replacement.
- **Supermarket commitments.** Section 8 says partners "will continue to offer" surplus. The cover note calls these "written commitments", but nothing in the document says they cover the 1.2 tonnes a week. Attach the letters, or state the volumes they commit to. Surplus schemes are normally best-efforts, so say so honestly.
- **Evidence the 1.2 tonnes is logged.** The cover note says you log every declined offer. The document doesn't. Say so in Section 2 and give the logging period. It is your strongest evidence and it is currently missing.
- **Quotes.** Two quotes were obtained for the cold room and electrics, but the van has a single dealer price. The cover note is accurate on this, but the document should not imply the whole budget was competitively tested. Consider noting what you checked for the van.
- **Distribution sites.** Food is chilled at the warehouse and then goes to three sites that open on different days. Say how it is kept cold once there, since the sites currently have only domestic fridges.
- **Capacity.** Say who will drive the van and handle about 62 extra tonnes a year with two part-time staff. Funders often ask about food safety training and temperature monitoring too.
- **Overclaim in Section 9.** "Permanently transforms" and "very low cost per meal" are stronger than the evidence supports. Let the corrected numbers speak.

## What's strong

- The need is evidenced, especially the declined-food figure and the parcel composition.
- The project is tightly scoped to that need.
- The budget is itemised and totals correctly, with a stated quote process.
- Outcomes are measurable (parcels with fresh produce from under 10% to a target of 80%).

## My recommendation

Don't send as is. Once the three must-fix items are sorted, particularly the running-cost plan, this would be a much stronger application. I can draft revised wording for Sections 2, 3, 5, 7 and 8 if you tell me how the running costs will be covered.
